title: C passes everything by value -- so how does swap work?
description:
C hands every function a copy of your argument, so a normal function can't change a caller's variable. This Short walks through the classic swap: pass the addresses instead of the values, dereference the pointers, and the function reaches back and rewrites x and y in main. Drop the ampersands and you're just swapping two throwaway copies.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/06-pointers-basics/

#Shorts

beats.narration: In C, a function can't touch your variable. You pass in x, the function gets a copy, and your original never changes. So how does a swap function actually work?
The trick: don't pass the values, pass their addresses. swap takes two int pointers. The star means go to that address and change what's really stored there.
Now it works. swap reached back through those addresses and rewrote x and y in main. Drop the ampersands and you'd just swap two copies that get thrown away.

display.output:
Before swap: x=5, y=10
After swap:  x=10, y=5

beats.narration: That's pass by reference in C. If a function needs to change your variable, hand it a pointer. Otherwise it's only editing a copy.

display.heading: The rule
display.subheading: need to change it? pass a pointer
